items.note: Mosque inscription states it was built during the reign of Ghiyasuddin Khalji of the Malwa Sultanate; OCR damaged.
Mosque niches with elaborate borders; central roof stone has a motif of nine fishes (OCR rough).
Mosque described as a state-protected monument restored with parapet stones in the past.
Daulat Rai Mathur Haveli east of the Raja/Udayaditya palace; privately owned, cared for by the 6th generation of the family (OCR garbled).
Haveli spread over 12 courtyards, mostly ruined; central courtyard has a temple with Vishnu, Shiva-Parvati and Ganesha sculptures.
Uday Sagar water body on the outskirts of the village, with GPS position given.
Legend fragment: the dancer later came to be known as 'Benji Maada', linked with a temple near Udayasagar (OCR very garbled).

claim.value: dancer later known as Benji Maada, temple near Udayasagar

items.note: Stepwell shaft walls carved with animal and floral motifs; brackets for drawing water; described as unprotected and prone to rough use.
Inscription on the inner lintel of the pavilion; used by locals to fetch water (OCR garbled).
Udaypur and neighbouring villages are famous for sculptures of the 10th-11th century CE (OCR garbled).
Neighbouring village Mahuli: Vidisha district, 14 km from Basoda, 61 km from Vidisha, about 25 households and 125 people.
Village in Basoda Tehsil, 3 km south-west of Udaypur, on a river bank; sculptures found in the river bed at two different times.
Standing Vishnu sculpture, about six feet high, in red sandstone with decorative back panel.
Vishnu shown in Bhoga form; sculpture dated to the 11th century CE.
Sculpture of Shiva and Parvati (Figure 237) carved with Gandharvas on the back panel (OCR garbled).
Back panel carved with the vehicles of both deities, Nandi and a tiger (OCR garbled).
Varaha sculpture (Figure 248) in the precinct of a temple in Muradpur village (OCR garbled).
Varaha in grey stone, about seven feet long, six feet high, dated to the 11th century CE.
Damaged Earth figure beside the boar; tusk kept short, which makes it differ from other Varaha sculptures of the region.
